graduation_requirements.raw_text: Graduation Requirements Class of 2027 The completion of a minimum of 34 credits is required with the following distribution: English, Math, Science, Global Citizenship, and Electives require six (6) credits in each subject area; Physical Education requires two (2) credits; Health, Visual/Performing Arts require one (1) credit each.

courses.description: Students will practice comprehension, analysis, and synthesis within their reading through various activities with independent, guided, and required texts. Students will produce clear and coherent writing for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences, including Informative, argumentative and narrative writing. Students will participate effectively in a range of discussions, responding thoughtfully to diverse perspectives and expressing ideas clearly and persuasively. Students will also acquire and practice vocabulary throughout the course.
courses.fulfills_text: All ninth graders will take the year-long ninth grade English course.

courses.description: Students in American Literature will explore one or more themes about the American Experience portrayed by a variety of American writers. Examples of themes include place-based literature, socio-political writing, and What does it mean to be American? Students will read closely, craft thoughtful argumentative essays, make oral presentations, and write some narratives. Students will also acquire and practice vocabulary throughout the course.
courses.fulfills_text: Tenth graders will take year-long American Literature.

courses.description: European Literature explores a variety of classics from England and Europe, deepening students' analysis and synthesis of literature. We will focus primarily on argumentative writing. Students will also write personal narratives that they may develop into college essays. Students will make at least one presentation during the semester based on individual research. Students will also acquire and practice vocabulary throughout the course.

Students will read and analyze a variety of speculative, dystopian, and science fiction, examining author’s craft and how an author uses speculative, science fiction, and dystopian genres to examine significant real-world concerns. Students will write several short informative pieces examining these techniques and will use what they have learned to generate extended narratives.

The class focuses on the study, interpretation, and analysis of challenging literary texts, in multiple genres, including novels, short fiction, drama and poetry, in preparation for the Advanced Placement English Literature Exam as well as for college level courses in literature and composition. Students use the language of literary analysis and criticism in discussing, building understanding, and writing about literature to meet proficiency in argumentative and narrative writing, as well as reading. Students expand their repertoire of literary terms with which to engage in thoughtful analysis and interpretation through questioning, writing, speaking and listening. Students will also acquire and practice vocabulary throughout the course.

In this course students will explore their creative expression. This process asks students to connect to their own creative voice through a variety of writing prompts, culminating in multiple short or one extended and revised narrative. Students will also learn to read like a writer, following their own reading interests. The class will also focus on speaking and listening as peers share their writing. Students will practice showing respect while giving feedback to help their peers in the writing and editing process.

In Journalism/Media Literacy students learn about the basics of journalism; consider and discuss the responsibilities and ethics of journalists; and produce a digital school publication (The Peoples Press). This involves conducting research and interviews, creating podcasts and vlogs, writing, editing, and revising. Students will also assess informative writing with a focus on how to engage readers. In the media literacy segment of the course, students will examine, speak about, and write about assessing credible news sources and identifying bias.

Students will read a wide range of poetry by authors of varying eras and countries. We will study poetic techniques and devices, such as rhyme, meter, alliteration, and metaphor, and practice these by writing our own poems. Students will write argumentative essays about poetry as well. Students will have opportunities to recite/perform original work and/or the work of others. Students will respectfully discuss their and others’ work in small groups and as a class.

Students will practice public speaking using multiple genres for sources, such as novels, poetry, speeches (famous and unknown), movies, music, monologues, eulogies, etc. At times, students will write their own material for speeches. Each performance will be assessed for vocal control (volume, pacing, enunciation) gestures (body and face), and eye contact. We will attempt to have live audiences for as many performances as possible.

This course will examine the content of world history from the Prehistoric through the First Empires. In each unit students will discover and show their understanding of how the civilization under study developed key concepts in history, civics, geography and economics. Students will do this while building their historical inquiry skills of developing good questions, analyzing sources and developing claims supported with solid evidence. In each unit students will apply their inquiry and communication skills to individual projects that let them follow their own interests in making connections to history, civics, economics and geography.
courses.fulfills_text: The expectation is that students will take World History I and II as well as US History prior to enrollment in other Global Citizenship courses.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Historical Inquiry, History, Geography

courses.description: This course will examine the periods of Reformation and the Scientific Revolution; the ages of discovery and the impact of European colonization of the Americas and Africa. Lastly it examines the periods of democratic revolutions in England and France that set the stage for the birth of the United States. In each unit students will discover and show their understanding of how the civilization developed key concepts in history, civics, geography and economics. Students will do this while building their historical inquiry skills of developing good questions, analyzing sources and developing claims supported with solid evidence. In each unit students will apply their inquiry and communication skills to individual projects that let them follow their own interests in making connections to history, civics, economics and geography.
courses.fulfills_text: The expectation is that students will take World History I and II as well as US History prior to enrollment in other Global Citizenship courses.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Historical Inquiry, History, Geography, Civics, Economics

courses.description: Students will study United States History from the Pre-Columbian Era through the Modern Era with a focus on the development of the government. Special emphasis is placed on teaching and learning United States history from a variety of voices and perspectives. Students will be asked to analyze how our past informs our decision making today. All students will be given opportunities to pursue areas of personal interests.
courses.fulfills_text: The expectation is that students will take World History I and II as well as US History prior to enrollment in other Global Citizenship courses.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Historical Inquiry, History, Geography, Civics, Economics

courses.description: Global Cuisine is a hands-on, interdisciplinary high school course that explores foods from around the world through historical, cultural, and economic perspectives. Students will investigate how geography, trade, migration, colonization, and cultural exchange have shaped the foods we eat today. Through cooking labs, food tastings, and collaborative projects, students will learn about the evolution of traditional dishes, the blending of cultures that create new cuisines, and the ways food reflects identity and community. This course emphasizes experiential learning as students prepare dishes from diverse regions, analyze the global food system, and examine how food connects people across cultures and time. Students will also explore topics such as food sustainability, access, and globalization, gaining an appreciation for the role food plays in bringing people together and shaping shared human experiences. By the end of the course, students will develop practical culinary skills, cultural awareness, and a deeper understanding of the powerful connections between food, history, and society.
courses.notes: Learning Objective Historical Inquiry, History, Geography,

courses.description: Music and Movements will explore revolutions in music, fashion, language, art, film and more. Students will explore bands and artists such as the Beatles, Jimi Hendrix, and Beyonce. Analyze changes in fashion over the decades, the evolution of film and its impact on society, as well as art exploration throughout the ages.
courses.notes: Learning Objective Historical Inquiry, History, Civics

courses.description: This AP course is a year-long exploration of behavior and mental processes. Students will have the option of taking the AP exam in May. The course is a deeper dive into the same concepts as the semester-long Introduction to Psychology course so students who have already taken the course can expect for some of the course to be a review of that material. This AP course and exam focus on key overarching ideas in human and animal thinking and behavior and applying all of the concepts and terms to everyday life. Explore the ideas, theories, and methods of the scientific study of behavior and mental processes. Students will examine the concepts of psychology through reading and discussion and students will analyze data from psychological research studies.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Inquiry, History, Civics, Geography (Culture)

courses.description: The AP United States History course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of American history from the pre-Columbian era to the present day. The course aims to develop students' abilities to think critically, analyze historical events and evidence, and express historical arguments both in writing and verbally. Students will be asked to think critically through different perspectives throughout the course of US History and understand the impact history has on our present. This course will require a time commitment and ask students to go above and beyond the scope of high school learning, and dive into college level curriculum, reading, and analysis.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Historical Inquiry, History, Geography, Civics, Economics

courses.description: Psychology is the study of thinking and behavior and in this course we will focus heavily on human thinking and behavior. Students will study a variety of topics covered in an introductory psychology course, including a history of psychological theories, psychological research methods, learning, cognition, motivation, emotion, memory and personality. Students will practice inquiry and research skills, using a variety of psychological perspectives to analyze human behavior, and practice their writing and public speaking skills.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Historical Inquiry, History, Geography (Culture), Civics

courses.description: Sociology is the study of human groups. Sociology’s topics range from crime to religion, from the family to the state, from the divisions of race and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture, and from social stability to radical change in whole societies. A common theme is sociology’s purpose of understanding how human action and consciousness both shape and are shaped by surrounding cultural and social structures. Students will practice the skills of inquiry, geography, civics, and history.
courses.notes: Learning Objective Inquiry, History, Civics; Geography, Economics

courses.description: Students will learn basic economic concepts, market systems, monetary and fiscal policy in order to apply them to solving both personal and national issues. The course consists of 3 units where we explore the basics of resources and incentives; free and command market systems, and finally the business cycle and monetary and fiscal policy. Learning activities rely on class readings, simulations, case studies and current events.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Historical Inquiry, Economics

courses.description: This course builds on U.S. History and the history department recommends that students take U.S. History prior to taking this course. Civics is an introductory course in which students cultivate their understanding of U.S. government and politics. This course is designed to prepare students for their rights as a citizen in our democracy by teaching them the constitutional rules of our government, how to select and elect representatives and how to participate in our government. Students will be assessed in a variety of reading and class activities as well as participation in a class action project.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Historical Inquiry, Civics

courses.course_name: Next Steps: Career Readiness & Financial Literacy
courses.description: In this class, students will be exploring topics related to career readiness (career exploration, resume writing, interview skills, etc) and personal finance. Units related to personal finance include banking, taxes, investing, retirement, managing credit, budgeting, and insurance.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Career Readiness, Banking, Managing Credit, Savings and Investing, Budgeting, Taxes, Insurance.

courses.description: Integrated Science 9 is a yearlong course broken up into two semesters. Semester one focuses on environmental science and introductory chemistry. Students will focus their studies around the nature of planet Earth, while learning fundamental concepts in chemistry as well as some biology. An overarching theme of these units is human sustainability - how we impact the earth and positive solutions to certain human driven issues. Students will also learn about basic concepts in chemistry such as experimental design, atomic structure, and chemical reactions. The second semester of the source covers concepts in space science, introductory physics and engineering. Students study the properties and behaviors of light (a.k.a. electromagnetic radiation). Students study how light provides evidence for the creation of the universe through learning about evidence supporting the big bang theory. In this section students will also study the basics of star formation and the formation of the solar system. Students also learn about concepts related to physics. Students learn about different types of energy, with a focus on mechanical energy. Students study Newton’s laws by researching and designing their own engineering projects. The course is primarily taught through lectures, discussions, videos, labs, and self-guided research. Throughout the course, students will be expected to develop three fundamental skills in science: investigating, analyzing, and communicating.
courses.fulfills_text: All students are required to take Integrated Science 9, Biology and Chemistry

courses.description: Biology is the detailed study of life. Students will explore the structure and function of organisms, and how energy flows and matter cycles within them. Students will make many connections between biology at the cellular level and biology at the organism level. Students will explore genetics, evolution and the interdependence of life on earth. Students will note how life continuously changes over time with respect to specific environments. Students will design and conduct their own experiments to investigate science concepts and develop their understanding. Prerequisite: Having passed Integrated Science 9.
courses.fulfills_text: All students are required to take Integrated Science 9, Biology and Chemistry

courses.description: Chemistry is the study of matter and the changes it undergoes. It’s the way the world works! Chemistry is useful for a strong background in biology, as well as earth and environmental sciences. This course is a prerequisite for AP Biology and AP Chemistry. The course has four themes: 1. Matter comes in various forms 2. Matter has unique properties 3. Matter can change 4. Interactions between matter are predictable. Students will explore these themes through laboratory experiments and hands-on inquiry activities. Prerequisite: Having passed Integrated Science 9.
courses.fulfills_text: All students are required to take Integrated Science 9, Biology and Chemistry

courses.description: The theme of this course is “the way things move, and why things move.” Learn to describe the motion (kinematics) of objects using words, mathematical equations, and graphs in one and two dimensions. Learn to describe the forces (dynamics) acting on an object in one and two dimensions using vector diagrams and mathematical relationships. Explore conservation of energy to predict the motion of falling and launched objects. Prerequisite: Having passed Integrated Science 9, Algebra AND Trigonometry.
courses.prerequisites: Having passed Integrated Science 9, Algebra AND Trigonometry.

courses.description: Explore electrostatics, electric current, and electromagnetism in this course. The course begins with a focus on the properties of electric forces and electric fields. Then students will learn about electric current, voltage, and resistance through hands-on activities and circuit analysis. Magnetism follows, along with electromagnetic induction, with applications in motors, electromagnets, and many of our technological devices. The course ends with an exploration of solar electricity generation and how solar differs from electromagnetic induction. Prerequisite: Having passed Integrated Science 9 AND Algebra
courses.prerequisites: Having passed Integrated Science 9 AND Algebra

courses.description: Advanced Placement Environmental Science (APES) is an introductory level college course which integrates student learning in Integrated Science, Biology, Chemistry, and Advanced Algebra classes. Students improve systems thinking and model Earth’s integrated systems by synthesizing human and natural influences on planetary systems. Throughout the course, students regularly do extensive field work, labs, text readings, hw assignments and improve scores on practice APES exams throughout the year. Students are expected to perform well on the APES exam in May. Prerequisite: Having passed Integrated Science 9, AND/OR Biology or Chemistry
courses.prerequisites: Having passed Integrated Science 9, AND/OR Biology or Chemistry

courses.description: Students will learn the parts of the human body and the body systems they belong to. They will then decipher how all of these body systems conveniently work together, allowing us to go about our daily life processes. Students will complete labs, interview health care providers, and have multiple guest speakers. They will also write a scientific, literary review on a topic of their choice.. Prerequisite: Students will have had to pass Biology or Chemistry as a Sophomore.
courses.prerequisites: Students will have had to pass Biology or Chemistry as a Sophomore.

courses.description: Students will explore the basics of astronomy. Our understanding of the solar system, our local group of galaxies, and the universe as a whole will be discussed in this interesting and exciting semester-long science elective. The class is split into various units related to the study of astronomy. Students will begin by learning how to identify various objects in the night sky through knowledge of the constellations as well as through the use of a telescope. Students will have the opportunity to utilize the Grout Observatory for special observing nights. Students will learn about the multiple types of telescopes and astronomical instruments used to discover information about what is beyond Earth’s atmosphere. The way data is collected and analyzed, and how that analysis furthers our understanding of the universe and our place within it, is an overarching theme of this course. They will also learn about the history of astronomy and the great lengths to which our understanding of the universe has expanded over time while developing an understanding of how much there is left to learn. Prerequisite: Having passed Integrated Science 9

S1. The course starts with learning the order of operations, simplifying fractions, and determining the prime factorization of numbers. Then, the course moves onto reasoning with ratios and rates. The students then revisit the order of operations where they work with integers instead of just working with natural numbers. Additionally, they work to further develop their number sense by ordering integers (relative magnitude). Next, the course moves on to the coordinate plane and linear relationships. The focus is on proportional relationships and constant rates of change. Finally, the students begin working with equivalent expressions and solving equations. S2. The course continues with solving more complex equations (compared to the first semester) and explores special cases (where the solution sets are no solution and all real numbers). Students will also solve inequalities and graph their solutions sets on the number line. Next, the students revisit linear relationships. This time learning the different types of slope, graphing and writing the equation of lines in slope-intercept form, and answering questions pertaining to word problems. Finally, the students begin working with systems of equations. They learn how to solve systems by graphing and the substitution method.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Common Core aligned formative and summative assessments, Learning Scales aligned to

courses.description: The graduation learning targets we will cover in Common Core Algebra are, Algebra, Functions, Statistics and Number, Quantity & Operations. The content standards which will be addressed for Algebra are: to interpret structure of expressions, write expressions in equivalent forms to solve problems, solve and create equations, solve systems of equations, and to graph inequalities and equations. For Functions the content standards are: to understand the concept of a function and use of function notation, and to analyze functions using different representations. In Statistics the content standards are: to summarize, represent, and interpret data. Finally, in Number, Quantity, and Operations the content standard is to reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Algebra: Graphing; Algebra: Expression; Algebra: Equations and Inequalities; Functions: Understanding and Analyzing; Numbers, Quantity & Operations: Number Sense & Operations

courses.description: The content standards we cover in Geometry are to make geometric constructions, experiment with transformations, prove geometric theorems, understand similarity and congruence. The course covers understanding and applying theorems about circles including arc lengths and areas of sectors. Finally, the focus will be on defining trigonometric ratios and using them to solve problems involving right triangles.
courses.notes: Domains: Geometry: Properties, Constructions and Modeling; Geometry:Congruence & Transformations; Geometry: Similarity and Trigonometry; Numbers, Quantity & Operations: Number Sense & Operations

courses.description: Students will develop a deep understanding of mathematical functions. Students will become proficient in using function notation to communicate their mathematical thinking and they will learn to analyze functions graphically, numerically, and analytically. Students will learn the characteristics of quadratic and polynomial functions, exponential and logarithmic functions, rational functions, and circular functions, and students will use these functions to model problems in the real world. Students will develop an understanding of how functions are created from other functions using mathematical operations, composition, and transformations, and be able to use this knowledge to analyze functions based on the functions’ origins. Students will also investigate ideas of statistics such as regression and probability.
courses.notes: Domains: Algebra: Expression; Algebra: Equations & Inequalities; Numbers, Quantity & Operations: Number Sense and Operations; Functions: Understanding & Analyzing; Functions: Building, Solving & Graphing

courses.description: AP Calculus AB is structured around three big ideas: limits, derivatives, and integrals. Students will evaluate limits graphically, numerically, and analytically and to use limits to analyze the graph of a function. Students will define the derivative as a limit and calculate the derivative of an explicitly defined function. They will also learn to use derivatives in a variety of applications including finding the instantaneous rate of change of a function and solving problems involving rectilinear motion. Students will learn to calculate the derivative of implicitly defined functions and of inverse functions and to use derivatives to solve related rate problems and to analyze the graph of a function. They will evaluate indefinite and learn to define the definite integral as a limit. Additionally, students will learn to apply integrals to solve problems involving area, volume, motion, and differential equations, and students will be able to demonstrate understanding of the relationship between derivatives and integrals as expressed in theFundamental Theorem of Calculus. Students may take the AP Calculus AB exam in the spring. A graphing calculator is required for this course.
courses.notes: Domains: Connecting Representations, Integration, Limits, Differentiation

courses.description: This course provides an introduction to the basic ideas and techniques of probability and statistics and of inferential procedures in statistics. Students will learn to summarize univariate data graphically and numerically with special emphasis on the normal model, and students will be able to create and analyze a least squares regression model for bivariate data. Students will design studies and experiments to answer questions and use probability sampling to collect data. Students will explore basic probability models. Students will be able to create and use probability models to answer questions and will be able to relate probability to sampling distribution models. Students will be able to apply sampling distribution models to the inference techniques of confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. Students who complete the year-long course may take the AP Statistics exam in the spring.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Collecting Data, Connecting Representations, Statistical Inference, Probability, Exploring Data

courses.description: This course explores many different math topics across the mathematics spectrum. Students will learn the principles of mathematical logic, basic set and number theory, counting methods and probability, consumer math, and basic principles of statistics and data analysis. Students will also review previously learned algebra and geometry skills as they apply these skills to problem-solving tasks.

Students will engage in conversations and provide information both orally and in writing. Students will perform skits, create stories, have conversations with the teacher and each other, and read two short novels. Communicating in another language leads to a deeper understanding of other cultures, their people, and their beliefs. There will be regular formative and summative quizzes on vocabulary and grammar concepts key to becoming proficient communicators.

Students communicate information by speaking and writing about familiar topics using multiple tenses and are able to identify and explain differences and similarities between their culture and the target culture(s). Students will engage in group, partner and individual work. They will use Spanish to perform skits, create stories, have conversations with the teacher and each other, present to the class, and read novels geared toward Spanish language learners along with short authentic pieces. There will be regular formative and summative quizzes on vocabulary and grammar concepts key to becoming a proficient communicator.

Students will engage in conversations, provide and obtain information both orally and in writing, express feelings, and exchange opinions. At this level, students will communicate in Spanish as we build a deeper understanding of the language and culture. Students will engage in group, partner, and individual work. They will perform skits, create stories, have conversations with the teacher and each other, and read two novels based on Latin American history. There will be regular formative and summative quizzes on vocabulary and grammar concepts key to becoming proficient communicators.

Students engage in conversations and communicate information about a variety of topics in detail, using culturally appropriate language. Students will engage in group, partner, and individual work. They will use Spanish to create movies, have detailed conversations about current events, present to the class, keep a journal and read authentic literature including short stories, legends, and plays. There will be formative and summative assessments on vocabulary and grammar concepts but the key to becoming proficient is their commitment to immersion in the Spanish language.

Students will understand meaning, engage in conversations, provide and obtain information both orally and in writing, express feelings, and exchange opinions. Students will understand that the effort to communicate in a foreign language leads to personal connections that provide a deeper understanding of other cultures, their people, and their beliefs. Students will engage in group, partner, and individual work. They will perform skits, create stories, have conversations with the teacher and each other,and read two short novels. There will be regular formative and summative quizzes on vocabulary and grammar concepts key to becoming proficient communicators.

Students communicate information and express their own thoughts about familiar topics using a series of sentences. Students engage in social interactions and conversations by asking and answering a variety of questions. Students can identify concrete examples of differences and similarities between their culture and the target cultures in Quebec. Students understand main ideas and some supporting details on familiar topics from a variety of sources. Students will demonstrate proficiency by engagement in group, partner and individual work. They will use French to perform skits, create stories, have conversations with the teacher and each other, present to the class, read novels geared toward French language learners along with short authentic samples. There will be regular formative and summative quizzes on vocabulary and grammar concepts key to becoming a proficient communicator.

Students will engage in conversations, provide and obtain information both orally and in writing,express feelings, and exchange opinions. Students will understand that the effort to communicate in a foreign language leads to personal connections that provide a deeper understanding of other cultures, their people, and their beliefs. Students will demonstrate proficiency by engagement in group, partner and individual work. They will use French to perform skits, create stories, have conversations with the teacher and each other, and read two short novels. There will be regular formative and summative quizzes on vocabulary and grammar concepts key to becoming proficient communicators.

Students engage in social interactions and conversations by asking and answering a variety of questions. Students understand main ideas and supporting details on topics from a variety of authentic sources. Students communicate information and express their own thoughts about topics in detail. Students use culturally appropriate target language to demonstrate their understanding of practices and perspectives. Students use peers and advanced or native speakers to practice and validate language use. Students will demonstrate proficiency by engagement in group, partner and individual work. They will use French to create movies, have detailed conversations about current events, present to the class,and read authentic literature. The final performance assessment in each unit will provide ongoing evidence of proficiency. Students will track their progress, conferencing with the teacher along the way.

Students will CREATE, CONNECT, PRESENT AND RESPOND TO their own visual artwork independently and collaboratively. Students will learn to express themselves and show understanding of a variety of art techniques. They will complete self-assessments and reflections about personal artwork as well as others' work. Students will also engage in class critiques (written and oral).

Students will CREATE, CONNECT, PRESENT AND RESPOND to their own visual artwork independently and collaboratively. Students will express themselves on a rigorous level, integrating personal experiences and original ideas with each project. Students will use prior knowledge of art techniques and applications in order to create thought provoking and expressive works. Students will write artist statements for each of their completed projects as well as present and engage in class critiques (written and oral).

Students will CREATE, CONNECT, PRESENT AND RESPOND to their own visual artwork independently and collaboratively. Students will create two different portfolios (totaling to at least 24 exemplary pieces of artwork) throughout the year to submit to the College Board for potential college credit. Students will choose between a DRAWING, 2D or 3D portfolio to execute throughout the school year. Students will express themselves on a rigorous level, integrating personal experiences and original ideas within each project. Students will use prior knowledge of art techniques and applications in order to create thought provoking and expressive works that show a high quality of craftsmanship. Students will write artist statements for each of their completed projects as well as present and engage in classroom critiques (written and oral).

Students will CREATE, CONNECT, PRESENT AND RESPOND to their own visual artwork independently and collaboratively. Students will express themselves on a rigorous level, integrating personal experiences in the style of various artists from the past and present from around the world. Students will be open minded and curious to learn about artists from across the globe, while incorporating these artists techniques and concepts into their own original ideas with each project. Students will use prior knowledge of art techniques and applications in order to create thought provoking and expressive works. Students will write artist statements for each of their completed projects as well as present and engage in class critiques (written and oral).

Students generate and conceptualize artistic ideas using a diversity of digital media including photography and graphic design. Through examining the elements and principles of photography and graphic design, students will learn how to create, reflect, and plan revisions for their work. Students examine artistic ideas and connect them to a historical and cultural context in order to understand how art influences ideas and emotions. Students develop, analyze, and select work for presentation while gaining an appreciation and knowledge of digital art methods and techniques. Artwork is evaluated based on specific criteria and responded to through critique.

Students explore and generate ideas using a diversity of ceramic methods and techniques including wheel throwing and handbuilding. The history of clay is examined as students analyze ceramic works from various cultures and connect those ideas to their personal work. Students apply artistic knowledge to analyze their own and others work through critique. Students gain an understanding of the importance of the artistic process through creating, refining, and presenting their work.

High School Chorus is open to all students interested in singing, regardless of prior experience. ● Students will present a large variety of vocal music from a wide range of popular genres in a performance setting. ● Students will learn how to use your voice effectively and sing in parts, unaccompanied and with instrumental backing. ● We will emphasize healthy vocal techniques as well as basic performance skills. ● Students will learn contemporary and traditional vocal literature in styles from classical to mainstream pop. ● We will work on reading music, tone production, basic vocal techniques, and working as a team in a performance. ● We will have numerous opportunities for students to audition for music festivals.

Concert Band provides instrumental performance experience. The band performs in various concerts and at commencement exercises and also comprises the Marching Band for civic events such as parades. ● Exposure to a variety of musical styles and musical periods. ● Students develop reading and performance skills through group rehearsals and individual practice ● Students participate in the various musical variety shows, school programs, community events, and small ensembles. ● Students are encouraged to participate in district and state music festival auditions. ● The band also competes biennially in national music festivals in different localities around the eastern US. We travel on off-years to New York City or Boston to provide a non-performing cultural experience

Students enrolled in this course will be focusing on the proficiency of recognizing the value of physical activity for health, enjoyment, challenge, self-expression and social interaction. Learning and understanding new ways to promote muscular strength, endurance, and flexibility will be implemented.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Movement/Physical Activity, Social Interactions: Applying Knowledge, Health/Wellbeing: Demonstrates Skills to Live Healthy Lifestyle, Personal/Social Responsibility.

courses.description: Students in physical education can select and participate in individual physical activities and/or team sports (softball, ultimate frisbee, soccer, etc..) to recognize the value of physical activity for health, enjoyment, challenge, self-expression and social interaction . Developing a warm and welcoming environment is emphasized, while participation is an aimed scholarly habit. Being productive and self-motivated in a group or individual choice activity will be established through practice and routines.
courses.notes: Learning Domains: Movement/Physical Activity, Social Interactions: Applying Knowledge, Health/Wellbeing: Demonstrates Skills to Live Healthy Lifestyle, Personal/Social Responsibility.

courses.description: The goal of Health Education is to help establish patterns of behavior that will assist a person in achieving complete health. Complete health is accomplished by having a balance of physical, mental, social, and emotional well-being. This course is designed to offer students the opportunity to acquire knowledge, incorporate process and life skills, and develop positive attitudes about life. Building a solid foundation of good decision-making skills can contribute to a variety of healthy choices for themselves and others. Development of a healthy body and a healthy mind will assist young people in living active, productive, and successful lives.
courses.notes: Domains: Core Concepts, Analyze Influences, Interpersonal Communication Skills

courses.description: Embark on an exciting journey into the realms of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM). This course fosters hands-on exploration, problem-solving, and collaboration. Dive into computer-aided design, real-world applications, fabrication, and projects of your own choosing, cultivating creativity, critical thinking, and innovation in the dynamic fields of STEM. If you would like to make or design objects that have a purpose; this is a course for you.
courses.notes: Domains: Understanding of Technology, Design Tool - Technical Creativity, Design Tool - Technical Illustration, Design Tools - Appropriate Tool and Material Use

courses.description: If you would like to make or design objects that have a purpose, ...this is a course for you. Immerse yourself in science, technology, engineering, arts, and math (STEAM). This course fosters hands-on exploration, problem-solving, and collaboration. Learn to use computer-aided design (CAD) software, study real-world applications and fabrication, and work with projects of your own choosing, all while cultivating creativity, critical thinking, and innovation in the dynamic fields of STEAM.
courses.notes: Domains: Understanding of Technology, Design Tools - Appropriate Tool and Material Use

courses.description: This course is designed to offer any student to work with tools and materials to solve technical problems or simply to build something they want or need for a school project or at home. There will be a focus on student initiative and project completion but students can elect to work on projects individually or in a team. If you sign up, you will work with a variety of hand and power tools and materials but also have the opportunity to use the 3d printer and laser cutter. Lots of choice here! Projects can range from building a basic wooden bookshelf to working with other students to design and construct a fully functional electric vehicle. Or anything in between. If you want it and we have the capability to do it, … let’s make it!
courses.notes: Domains: Understanding of Technology, Design Tool -Technical Creativity, Design Tools - Appropriate Tool and Material Use

courses.description: Driver Education will develop the physical, mental, and emotional skills needed to be a risk free driver. Special Note: Enrolled students must provide physical proof of state issued learner’s permit card with their name on the first day of class. Failure to do so will most likely result in being removed from the course. Those permits must remain free of points or other moving violations. Students will also be given a basic eye examination at the start of class through our school nurse. Any restrictions regarding corrective lenses must be followed at all times. Curriculum will be based on the Vermont Driver Risk Prevention and the Zone Control System. Course consists of five parts: 1. Classroom -- at least 30 hours 2. In-Car -- at least 6 hours of driving and 6 hours of observation completed in the Driver Education Vehicle. 3. Parent/Guardian -- 40 hours of supervised driving time -- 20 hours of this time should occur while a student is enrolled in the Driver Education Course (An additional 20 is recommended if the student has completed the 40 hours before enrolling in the course). 4. Parents attend mandatory meetings at the beginning of the semester. 5. Social Responsibility: (Student’s Attitudes and Behaviors). The act of driving is highly social. Students are expected to demonstrate proficiency in all the Scholarly Habits, with special attention given to Perseverance, Social Skills, and Mindset. Students must also demonstrate self control to think before they act, accept responsibility for their actions, participate in group discussions and follow the rules and laws in the school setting and in the outside community. According to state requirements, if absent, the student must make up for the missed class. Student will demonstrate proficiency: In-In Class & In Vehicle In-Class Demonstrate an understanding of Driving as a High Risk Activity Demonstrate knowledge of the laws, rules, and procedures of operating a vehicle Demonstrate an understanding of using visual perception skills to evaluate the traffic environment Demonstrates an understanding of positive interactions with other users of the Roadways Demonstrate an understanding of the importance of protecting self and others by using seat belts, controls, and personal safety skills Demonstrate an understanding of the importance of making healthy/safe choices regarding chemical, physical, and psycho-emotional factors Able to explain how vehicle maintenance and driver decisions impact the environment In-Vehicle: Demonstrate key in hand mindset -- “I am ready to drive” Able to see an open and safe path before putting the car in motion Interact courteously with others Able to keep vehicle in balance by making smooth, precise steering and speed adjustments Able to search and control all zones around the vehicle Able to control an intersection Able to safely make a lane change Able to complete all the requirements of the state road test Able to solve problems using Zone Control Actions Demonstrate a commitment to making healthy choices through risk prevention to ensure the safety of others and self

The Vermont Virtual Learning Cooperative (VTVLC) is an organization developed through a partnership of Vermont public schools which is funded by a grant provided by the Vermont Department of Education using ARRA/ Title IID funds. Programs and courses are available to all Vermont students; enrollment is prioritized based on school partnership status.

courses.description: Dual Enrollment vouchers allow juniors and seniors to take up to two college courses while still in high school. Students earn college credits, reducing the time it takes to get a college degree, potentially reducing the costs associated with college, and challenging themselves through college level curriculum. Courses can be online, on a college campus or taught at Peoples Academy. See your guidance counselor for assistance with the process. Students earn college credit and high school credit.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: Fast Forward is for Vermont students attending a technical center who want to earn college credits. Students earn credits at both the Technical Center and CCV or Vermont Tech. Courses are taught at the Technical Center and classes are scheduled during the regular school day. Students may be eligible for up to two free Technical Center Dual Enrollment courses. Additional courses cost $100
courses.notes: program

courses.description: This is a full year alternative to the senior year of high school Students take courses at college, completing their senior year of high school and their freshman year of college simultaneously. Programs are available at CCV, Castleton, Johnson State, Lyndon State, and Burlington College. Early College also includes the Vermont Academy of Science and Technology (VAST) at Vermont Tech.
